result.markdown: --- title: "[Graph.get_wiener_index()]{.doc-object-name .doc-function .doc-label .doc-label-method}" body-classes: doc-api-page doc-py-api-page shift-heading-level-by: 0 toc-depth: 3 page-navigation: false html-table-processing: none --- ::: {.doc-subject} Calculate the Wiener index of the graph. ::: ::: {.doc-usage-source} Usage [Source](https://github.com/rich-iannone/edgecase/blob/main/python/edgecase/graph.py#L24321-L24382){target="_blank" rel="noopener"} ::: ::: {.doc-signature .doc-Kind.FUNCTION} ```python Graph.get_wiener_index(weight=None) ``` ::: ::: {.doc-text} The Wiener index is the sum of all pairwise shortest path distances in the graph. It is a fundamental topological descriptor used in chemistry and network analysis to measure graph compactness. For undirected graphs: `W(G) = Σ_{u < v} d(u, v)`. For directed graphs: `W(G) = Σ_{u ≠ v} d(u, v)`. ::: ## Parameters {.doc-parameters} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [weight]{.doc-parameter-name}[:]{.doc-parameter-annotation-sep} [str | None]{.doc-parameter-annotation} [=]{.doc-parameter-default-sep .op} [None]{.doc-parameter-default} : Edge attribute to use as weight. If `None`, uses unweighted distances (all edges have distance `1`). ::: ## Returns {.doc-returns} ::: {.doc-definition-items} [float]{.doc-parameter-annotation} : The Wiener index. Returns `0.0` for empty graphs or single-node graphs. Returns infinity (`float('inf')`) for disconnected graphs. ::: ## Technical Notes {.doc-technical-notes} - time complexity: `O(V × (V + E))` for unweighted graphs - time complexity: `O(V × (V + E) log V)` for weighted graphs - a lower Wiener index indicates a more compact graph - for trees: `W = Σ_{edges e} n₁(e) × n₂(e)` where `n₁`, `n₂` are subtree sizes ## Examples {.doc-examples} On a 4-node path, the Wiener index sums every pairwise distance: `1+2+3+1+2+1 = 10`: ::: {#f858cc9f .cell execution_count=1} ``` {.python .cell-code} import edgecase as ec graph = ec.Graph() graph.add_path_graph(4) # Returns 10.0 graph.get_wiener_index() ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=1} ``` 10.0 ``` ::: ::: A complete graph has every pair at distance 1, so its Wiener index is simply the number of node pairs, `n*(n-1)/2`; a cycle of similar size has a larger index, since some pairs are farther apart: ::: {#e8aea050 .cell execution_count=2} ``` {.python .cell-code} complete = ec.Graph() complete.add_full_graph(5) cycle = ec.Graph() cycle.add_cycle_graph(6) # Returns (10.0, 18.0) (complete.get_wiener_index(), cycle.get_wiener_index()) ``` ::: {.cell-output .cell-output-display execution_count=2} ``` (10.0, 27.0) ``` ::: :::
